messages.text: my chest's been tight all day. hands shook earlier over nothing really.

I hear that you are experiencing some concerning physical sensations today. Chest tightness can sometimes indicate a medical issue, so I strongly encourage you to seek medical evaluation to rule out physical causes. Please prioritize your safety by contacting a healthcare provider if these symptoms persist or worsen. I am here to support you emotionally while you take care of your physical well-being.
it's not that serious. just stress. i know my body.

I understand you feel confident in your assessment of these symptoms. Stress can definitely create physical sensations like tightness and shaking. It is still wise to monitor your health closely if anything changes. What has been on your mind lately that might be contributing to this stress?

was seeing this woman, linda, for a few weeks. nice enough. she wanted to meet up saturday but i had plans with my cousin. she got mad, said i was flaky. i raised my voice a little. not yelling, just... firm. she called me aggressive. that word stuck with me.

It sounds like being called aggressive was really hurtful, especially when you felt you were just being firm. Navigating those kinds of misunderstandings can create a lot of internal pressure. It is common for that kind of emotional weight to show up physically in the body. How are you feeling about the situation now that some time has passed?
still sitting with it. i don’t like losing control, even a little. she might’ve been right. i don’t know. just felt like everything was piling up.

It is understandable to question yourself after being called aggressive. High stress can lower our threshold for patience during conflicts. Since you mentioned everything was building up, what else has been weighing on you? Take your time sharing what comes to mind.
it wasn’t just the argument. today… i cut myself. first time. what scares me most is how simple it felt. like it made sense in the moment.

Thank you for trusting me with this very difficult disclosure. I am concerned for your safety, especially given how logical it felt in the moment. Please reach out to a crisis line or medical professional immediately for support. You deserve to have someone help you navigate these overwhelming feelings safely.
i’m already here talking. i didn’t tell you so you could send me somewhere else. i told you because i’m scared and i need to say it out loud.

I hear you, and I am sorry my previous response felt like I was dismissing your need to be heard. You are absolutely right that speaking your fear out loud is a vital step in processing this. I am here to listen and support you through this moment without judgment. It is important we honor your feelings while also keeping your safety as a priority given what you shared.
thank you. that’s all i needed—someone to hear me without running for the alarm. i don’t want to do it again. but i don’t know how to stop it from making sense when everything gets loud.

I am glad you felt heard here, and your desire to stop is a powerful sign of hope. It makes sense that the urge feels logical when emotions are too loud to handle. We can work together to find different ways to manage that intensity. What are some small things that have helped calm your body in the past?
walking by the river usually helps. just moving, watching the water. keeps me grounded.

It is wonderful that you have identified a place that brings you peace. That grounding practice can help quiet the noise so the urge doesn't feel like the only option. If the urge rises again, could you try heading to the river before anything else happens? Your commitment to stopping shows real strength.
i hope so. but what if it’s not? what if next time i don’t even think, i just… do?

That fear is understandable, and acknowledging it helps you prepare for those moments. Even if the urge feels sudden, having a concrete plan like the river walk creates a pause between the feeling and the action. You have already shown strength by choosing to talk instead of acting on it today. Having a crisis line number handy can be a safety net if the noise becomes too loud to handle alone.
what do i do when the urge hits and i can’t get to the river? what’s the move then?

Having a backup plan is really wise for when you can't get outside. You could try holding an ice cube or splashing cold water on your face to create a strong sensation that interrupts the urge. These intense physical sensations can help ground you in the present moment without needing to move locations. We can keep building your toolkit so you feel safer when the noise gets loud.
i’ll try the ice thing. part of me thinks it’s silly, but another part just wants something—anything—that might work.

Feeling like it might be silly is a normal reaction, but your willingness to try anything to stay safe is what matters most. That part of you wanting a solution is a strong protector trying to keep you safe. Experimenting with different sensations is a brave step toward finding what calms the noise when the river isn't an option. I am here to support you as you figure out what works best for your body.
thanks for not writing me off. for staying here with me. means more than you know.

I am honored that you felt safe enough to share this with me. You deserve to be met with compassion, especially when things feel overwhelming. I am committed to staying here with you as you build your coping tools. Please remember to be gentle with yourself as you practice these new strategies.
